oneSentence: The rules, institutions and processes used to guide how AI is built, used and overseen so its benefits and risks are handled in the public interest.
plainExplanation:
AI governance is the practical system around AI: who sets expectations, who checks compliance, who is accountable, and how problems are addressed. It includes laws, policies, standards, oversight bodies, procurement rules, audits, reporting and ways for people to raise concerns.

What goes in? Many things: technical evidence about how a system works, reports of harm or benefit, public values, human rights concerns, security risks, market realities and the goals of governments, organisations and communities. In international settings, it also includes negotiation among Member States and input from companies, researchers and civil society.

What happens? People and institutions turn those inputs into guidance and decisions. They may write rules, agree principles, set technical standards, require testing, define responsibilities, limit certain uses, or create channels for review and redress. Governance is broader than regulation: regulation is one tool inside governance.

What comes out? Clearer expectations for developers, buyers, deployers and users of AI, plus mechanisms for oversight and correction. Good governance does not guarantee good outcomes, but it helps societies manage trade-offs, reduce harm, support useful innovation and make responsibility easier to trace when something goes wrong.

everydayAnalogy.title: Running a shared water system for several neighbourhoods
everydayAnalogy.story: Imagine several neighbourhoods share one water system. Engineers build the pipes, but the system also needs rules about water quality, meters, repairs, complaints, drought plans and who pays for upgrades. Residents, city officials, maintenance teams and health inspectors all play different roles. If a pipe bursts or water is contaminated, the system needs a way to detect it, respond quickly and decide who is responsible. The water system works best not just because pipes exist, but because the surrounding rules and institutions keep it reliable and fair.

mapping.analogyElement: Water quality rules, billing rules and inspection routines
mapping.aiElement: Policies, standards, audits and oversight requirements

mapping.analogyElement: Residents, engineers, inspectors and city officials
mapping.aiElement: Users, developers, regulators, organisations and public institutions

mapping.analogyElement: Complaint and repair process after a burst pipe
mapping.aiElement: Incident reporting, accountability and remedy when AI causes harm

everydayAnalogy.limitation: AI governance is not only about running one shared utility. AI systems are made by many actors across borders, change quickly, and are used in very different contexts such as health, education, finance and security. Unlike water quality, many AI questions involve contested values, uncertain evidence and trade-offs that cannot be solved by technical inspection alone.

visual.title: How AI governance turns concerns into oversight
visual.learningObjective: Show how evidence, values and institutions combine to produce rules, oversight and accountability for AI use.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with four stages. Read from inputs, to governance actions, to implementation, to outcomes. Each stage names what enters the process, what institutions do, and what kinds of results appear in practice.

steps.label: Inputs
steps.explanation: Evidence, public values, rights concerns, risks, benefits and practical needs enter the process.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a rounded rectangle on the left with six small icons or labels inside: evidence, rights, risks, benefits, public needs, market reality. Use arrows pointing right.

steps.label: Governance actions
steps.explanation: Authorities and organisations translate those inputs into laws, policies, standards, procurement rules and review processes.
steps.visualInstruction: Place a larger centre box labelled governance actions. Inside, list: laws, policies, standards, audits, procurement, reporting. Connect inputs to this box with a thick arrow.

steps.label: Implementation
steps.explanation: Developers, buyers and deployers apply those requirements through testing, documentation, monitoring and human oversight.
steps.visualInstruction: Add a third box to the right labelled implementation. Inside, show four checklist items: testing, documentation, monitoring, human oversight.

steps.label: Outcomes
steps.explanation: The result can include safer use, clearer accountability, fewer harms, and updates when new problems appear.
steps.visualInstruction: Add a final box on the far right labelled outcomes and feedback. Include labels: safer use, accountability, redress, revision. Draw a feedback arrow from this box back to governance actions.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each stage expands to show two examples: one public-sector example and one private-sector example.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram shows AI governance as a four-stage flow. First, inputs enter: evidence about system performance, public values, human rights concerns, possible risks, possible benefits and practical needs. Second, governance actions convert those inputs into rules and processes such as laws, policies, standards, audits, procurement requirements and reporting channels. Third, implementation applies those requirements through testing, documentation, monitoring and human oversight by the organisations that build or use AI. Fourth, outcomes include safer use, clearer accountability, remedies when harm occurs and revision of the rules when new problems are found. A feedback arrow from outcomes back to governance actions shows that governance is continuous, not one-time.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-column diagram with arrows between columns and one return arrow from outcomes to governance actions. No animation; all labels and examples are visible at once.

workedExample.scenario: An information management officer at Headquarters is finalising a concept note for an AI search assistant before clearance by an ICT governance board. The proposed pilot would search an approved collection of public reports and meeting records, returning relevant passages rather than unchecked summaries.
workedExample.input: Concept note: answer staff queries with links to source passages from an approved collection of public documents.
process: The concept note specifies the permitted purpose, users and document collection, and records uses that remain out of scope.
The business owner, technical owner and approving authority are named. Responsibility is assigned for testing, monitoring, incident handling and any decision to suspend the tool.
Procurement clauses require system documentation, notice of significant model changes, access controls, usage logs and a process for investigating reported errors.

Before deployment, staff test representative queries, misleading prompts and cases where the collection contains no answer. Responses must link to sources and state when the available evidence is insufficient.

After launch, the owner reviews error reports and usage patterns. Material failures trigger correction, user notification or suspension of the relevant function, not simply another reminder to check the output.
workedExample.result: The cleared concept note establishes authority, procurement conditions, testing, monitoring and remediation. Together, these arrangements form the governance framework for the pilot. The search feature is only the part colleagues see.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: By close of business, a programme officer in an evaluation office must complete the technical scoring of three bids for AI-assisted coding of interview notes and survey comments. The terms of reference require evidence on model limitations, data handling, human review, audit logs, incident reporting and correction of errors.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: AI governance is already operating through the evaluation criteria. Before a preferred bidder is identified, the panel can assess safeguards, allocate responsibilities and identify conditions for the contract, including testing, documentation, monitoring, reporting, suspension and remediation.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Bids, evaluator comments and evaluation evidence must not be entered into an AI tool unless it is approved for procurement-sensitive and personal information. An unapproved tool could expose confidential material, compromise the integrity of the evaluation and breach duties owed to interviewees or respondents.

whyItMatters: Non-specialists often meet AI governance before they meet advanced AI. It shapes what can be bought, deployed, restricted, reported and improved. If you help choose software, approve budgets, design services, draft policy or explain risks to leadership, governance determines the questions you should ask: Who is responsible? What checks exist? What evidence supports this system? How will problems be found and fixed? Without governance, AI use can become unclear, uneven and hard to challenge. With governance, decisions are more traceable, and organisations are better able to balance innovation, safety, rights and public trust.
whereYouMayHearIt: In General Assembly informals on draft text concerning AI
At a technical evaluation meeting for bids containing AI features
When an ICT governance board considers a pilot concept note
During clearance of an impact assessment before deployment
At a vendor demonstration when the discussion reaches accountability and incident handling

commonMisconceptions.misconception: AI governance just means passing an AI law.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Laws are only one part of governance. Governance also includes standards, procurement rules, oversight bodies, audits, reporting processes, professional guidance and practical ways to correct problems. An organisation can do some governance even before a new law exists.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: AI governance is only for governments.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Governments play a major role, but organisations, companies, standards bodies, researchers and civil society also shape how AI is used and checked. A hospital, school system or UN office may have internal governance responsibilities even when national rules are still developing.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a system is governed, it must be safe or fair.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Governance improves the chances of responsible use, but it does not guarantee good outcomes. Weak rules, poor enforcement, limited evidence or bad incentives can still lead to harm. Governance is a framework for managing risk and accountability, not a promise of perfection.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: AI governance is the set of rules and responsibilities around AI. It covers who may use it, what checks are required, and what happens if it causes problems.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: AI governance refers to the institutional, legal, procedural and operational arrangements that shape the design, development, procurement, deployment, oversight and remediation of AI systems. It can include binding and non-binding measures: legislation, regulation, standards, assurance mechanisms, impact assessment, procurement clauses, documentation duties, incident reporting, monitoring, redress and accountability allocation. In international discussion, the term may cover national governance, cross-border coordination and global processes involving states, international organisations, firms, technical communities and civil society. It is broader than regulation, broader than ethics guidance alone, and related to but distinct from AI safety, which usually focuses more narrowly on preventing specific forms of harm or failure.

keyTakeaway: AI governance is the surrounding system of rules, responsibilities and checks for building, buying and using AI, including what happens when the system fails.

quickCheck.question: Which example best shows AI governance rather than only building an AI system?
options: Training a model on satellite images to detect road damage
Buying software and requiring testing reports, human review, error logging and a complaint process
Making a faster computer chip for AI workloads
Using AI once to draft a meeting note
quickCheck.explanation: Governance is about the rules, oversight and accountability around AI use. The second option adds procurement conditions, review steps and ways to detect and respond to problems, which are governance mechanisms.

searchKeywords: difference between ai governance and regulation
contested: The broad idea is widely used, but the exact scope of AI governance is contested. Some people use it narrowly for government rule-making, while others include corporate governance, technical standards, international coordination and informal norms.

issues.problem: The claim that governance "makes AI use accountable" presents a guaranteed result. The page itself correctly says that weak rules or enforcement can still produce harm and that governance does not guarantee good outcomes.
issues.fix: AI governance is the surrounding system of rules, roles and checks intended to make AI use more accountable, not just the technology itself.

issues.problem: The final sentence again treats the presence of governance as sufficient to make decisions traceable and balance competing goals. Those benefits depend on the quality and implementation of governance.
issues.fix: Replace the final sentence with: "With effective governance, decisions can be more traceable, and organisations can be better able to balance innovation, safety, rights and public trust."

issues.problem: The example identifies both false alerts and missed damage as risks, but reports only precision. Precision concerns the proportion of flags that are correct. It does not measure missed damage and is not interchangeable with accuracy. The sequence therefore does not demonstrate that the stated "accuracy testing" requirement covers the identified risks.
issues.fix: Change "accuracy testing" to "performance testing". Replace the third step with: "Tests on 5,000 labelled images report false-alert and missed-damage rates, with weaker performance on unpaved roads."

issues.problem: The distinction from AI ethics is reduced to being broader than "ethics guidance alone", but the supplied definition describes AI ethics as a practice, not merely guidance. The distinction from AI safety is also vague. Governance concerns institutional rules, roles and accountability, while ethics checks normative qualities and safety focuses on reducing harm through design, testing and use.
